note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · FUZZY RABBIT-FOOT HEAD
tiles.details: Find a tightly contracted, often lobed panicle approximately 1.5–16 cm long; the soft halo is a useful first clue, not a species-level proof. Existing panels show the real fuzzy head and moist-site colony, not attached roots.
tiles.short: Dense pale-green or tawny awned panicle on a cool-season annual

tiles.heading: 02 · TRUE COLLAR
tiles.details: Open the true blade–sheath junction. Existing exact-species collar photographs in panels 2–3 show real translucent membranous tissue and adjacent blade/sheath from two angles; neither has a calibrated millimeter ruler, so do not assert a measured ligule length from these images. Published botanical treatments give a membranous ligule approximately 2.5–16 mm. The Setaria look-alike has a hair-fringed ligule; inspect the actual inner free edge rather than surrounding sheath hairs.
tiles.short: Membranous ligule, not the Setaria hair fringe

tiles.heading: 03 · TWO NOTCHED GLUMES
tiles.details: The mature spikelet body is about 2–3 mm EXCLUDING awns. Two similar keeled, one-veined glumes end in shallow notches, each bearing a roughly 4–10 mm awn (Kew commonly 4–7 mm). A fuzzy halo photo cannot prove the precise awn insertions.
tiles.short: Each tiny one-flowered spikelet has TWO glumes with long awns
tiles.status: ACTUAL AWN HALO — GLUME INSERTIONS NEED MACRO

tiles.heading: 04 · TINY INNER FERTILE LEMMA
tiles.details: Inside the two long-awned notched glumes is ONE fertile floret with a much smaller roughly 1–1.5 mm lemma, about five subtle veins, and a small palea. A short lemma awn may be present or absent (often 0–2 mm); do not teach it as always awnless. Panel 0 is a real loosened awned reproductive view, but the tiny lemma, palea and precise awn insertions are NOT independently isolated or measured there; a calibrated dissection is still missing.
tiles.short: The inner lemma is much shorter and can carry its OWN short awn

tiles.heading: 05 · ROOTED ANNUAL FORM
tiles.details: Photograph the whole verified plant with the flowering head attached, plus fibrous crown and lower culm nodes. Moist ditch habitat supports a search but is not identification; existing colony photos do not prove rooted annual anatomy.
tiles.short: Confirm a fibrous-rooted annual, sometimes with low bent or rooting nodes

tiles.heading: 06 · FOLLOW THE BRISTLE ORIGIN
tiles.details: Actual SAME SPECIES Polypogon indices 0–1 photograph long spikelet/glume awns and actual separated awned structures, but NOT clean split glume and lemma dissection. Photos 7–8 are genuine OTHER-species native *Setaria parviflora* whole foxtail and source-scaled bristle-origin macro, independently CC BY-SA4 and physically archived in Setaria canonical folder. Setaria bristles are below each spikelet; Polypogon long awns are FROM two glumes. Do not use Setaria images as Polypogon anatomy, and do not infer Hays native locality from photographs taken overseas. Need verified actual single mature Polypogon spikelet with both notched glumes and tiny fertile lemma separately shown at scale.
tiles.short: Polypogon awns grow from glumes; Setaria bristles from sterile branchlets
tiles.status: NATIVE SETARIA FOXTail COMPARISON NOW PHOTO-COVERED — GENUINE GLOME/LEMMA DISSECTION OPEN

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: ANNUAL BEARDGRASS / RABBIT'S-FOOT GRASS: in damp ditches and disturbed soils look for a short-to-medium ANNUAL grass with a dense, soft, pale-green to tawny cylindrical or lobed flowerhead. The fluffy HALO comes chiefly from TWO long awns (typically 4–10 mm) arising from notched tips of the TWO GLUMES around each tiny one-flowered spikelet. The much smaller fertile lemma can ALSO bear a short awn: NEVER teach 'glumes awned, lemma always awnless.' Separate introduced Setaria by bristle origin (sterile branchlets beneath spikelets), and Carolina Phalaris by compact firm glumes without this long awn halo.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Open the true blade–sheath junction. Existing exact-species collar photographs in panels 2–3 show real translucent membranous tissue and adjacent blade/sheath from two angles; neither has a calibrated millimeter ruler, so do not assert a measured ligule length from these images. Published botanical treatments give a membranous ligule approximately 2.5–16 mm. The Setaria look-alike has a hair-fringed ligule; inspect the actual inner free edge rather than surrounding sheath hairs.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: The mature spikelet body is about 2–3 mm EXCLUDING awns. Two similar keeled, one-veined glumes end in shallow notches, each bearing a roughly 4–10 mm awn (Kew commonly 4–7 mm). A fuzzy halo photo cannot prove the precise awn insertions.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Phalaris caroliniana: firm smooth-sided head of overlapping broad strongly keeled glumes, WITHOUT Polypogon's halo of long fine awns. Setaria parviflora/foxtails: bristles arise from modified sterile BRANCHES beneath spikelets, unlike TWO long AWNS attached to notched Polypogon GLUMES; Setaria also has hair-fringed ligule. Polypogon viridis: related grass without long awns on glumes, often creeping perennial. Phleum pratense: much shorter glume awns, lemma unawned, dense firmer timothy head. Alopecurus: often a short lemma awn, usually glumes without the conspicuous paired long awns of P. monspeliensis. Examine attachment, not mere fuzzy color.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: Annual beardgrass — detached spikelets with unusually long awns
panels.caption: Real sourced photograph shows widely separated small pointed green-brown reproductive units and very long thin pale awns, including two long awned structures near the left of the frame. It makes the awns' enormous length relative to tiny spikelet bodies easy to learn. Pixel resolution is insufficient to identify the notch of each individual glume or distinguish the inner lemma from a glume. Don't confuse this with Setaria's sterile-branch bristles.

panels.label: Annual beardgrass — real close reproductive branch and awns
panels.caption: Daniel Cahen's original photo shows two adjacent branchlets bearing narrow green reproductive structures with very long pale awns. The long projections are consistent with beardgrass's diagnostic awned glumes, but the attachment notch of each awn on a single isolated glume is NOT clear. Do not label a fertile lemma or claim verified paired glumes from this image.

panels.label: Annual beardgrass — translucent blade/sheath collar membrane
panels.caption: Daniel Cahen's photo shows a pale transparent, pointed membrane rising at a green blade-sheath junction on an upright stem. An upper sheath margin overlaps part of the base, and a nearby grass panicle is blurred. The exact free inner ligule margin and length cannot be measured: this is a close collar-location lesson, not proof of a 2.5–16 mm ligule.

panels.label: ANNUAL BEARDGRASS — Texas macro of fuzzy glume-awn halo
panels.caption: Annika Lindqvist's Texas photograph makes the many pale hairlike projections around this green, occasionally interrupted cylindrical head obvious. These are the GLUME AWNS responsible for the fuzzy appearance, but the precise junction of an awn with an individual split glume is NOT resolved here. The site was North Texas, not a Hays specimen.

panels.label: ANNUAL BEARDGRASS — colony of fuzzy panicles by shallow water
panels.caption: In this habitat view, several pale green fuzzy heads stand on thin stems at the edge of shallow water. Soil wetness helps crews decide where to LOOK, not what the exact species must be. Whole roots, membranous ligule and detached awned glumes remain unphotographed.
panels.creator: Andrey Zharkikh

panels.label: NATIVE LOOK-ALIKE — knotroot bristlegrass has bristles BELOW its spikelets
panels.caption: DIFFERENT PLANT: Native knotroot bristlegrass (*Setaria parviflora*) has dense cylindrical foxtail flowering heads in a living clump. Polypogon monspeliensis is introduced and can appear similarly fuzzy, but its abundant long awns extend from SPIKELET GLUMES, while Setaria's persistent bristles are inserted BELOW the spikelets. This source-identified non-Texas plant does not establish BONAP Hays occurrence by itself.
panels.creator: Stefan.lefnaer
panels.modifications: Scaled 3000x4000 authored image to 2400px longest side; oriented RGB and stripped EXIF/GPS; original photo not cropped, separate non-destructive browser-arrow overlays

panels.label: NATIVE LOOK-ALIKE MACRO — bristles below a Setaria spikelet, NOT Polypogon glume awns
panels.caption: DIFFERENT TAXON: Photographer's Setaria parviflora close-up shows bristles originating at the base BELOW a spikelet, with purple flowering parts and original 3-mm photograph scale. Contrast Polypogon where each glume bears its own long slender awn from the notched glume tip. Source photographer recorded Croatia; this is NOT Polypogon anatomy and not proof of Hays occurrence.

memory_rule: POLYPOGON = TWO LONG AWNED GLUMES per one-flowered spikelet + SHORT lemma (sometimes ALSO short-awned). SETARIA = bristles beneath spikelets from sterile branches. PHALARIS = broader firm glumes, no rabbit-foot fuzz.

Polypogon viridis: related grass without long awns on glumes, often creeping perennial. Phleum pratense: much shorter glume awns, lemma unawned, dense firmer timothy head. Alopecurus: often a short lemma awn, usually glumes without the conspicuous paired long awns of P. monspeliensis. Examine attachment, not mere fuzzy color.
